n: David waited and waited — and then God bent down and heard his cry. Patient waiting is rewarded.

f.g: Literally “waiting I waited” — a Hebrew way of stressing long, steady waiting.

n: God pulled him out of a muddy pit where he was sinking and set him on solid rock. Many see this as a picture of rescue from sin and death through Christ.

f.g: Thick, sucking mud — like the bottom of a cistern.

f.w: set my feet upon a rock

n: Deliverance gives him a new song of praise. When others see what God did, they too will reverence and trust him.
Blessed is the one who trusts the Lord rather than looking up to arrogant people or those who follow lies.

f.g: Go after false gods or falsehoods.

n: God’s wonders and his thoughtful plans for us are so many that no one could ever list them all.
God isn’t ultimately after animal sacrifices; he wants an obedient, listening heart. “Mine ears hast thou opened” means God has made him able to hear and obey.

f.w: Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire

f.g: Literally “ears you have dug for me.” The Greek Old Testament reads “a body you have prepared me,” which Hebrews 10:5 quotes.

n: “Here I am; I have come.” Hebrews applies these words to Jesus, who came to do the Father’s will, as written of him in the scroll.

f.g: The scroll — the written law or scripture.

n: True obedience is joyful and inward: God’s law lives in the heart. This perfectly describes Christ, who always did his Father’s will.

f.w: I delight to do thy will
thy law is within my heart

n: David has openly proclaimed God’s goodness before the gathered people, not keeping quiet.
He hasn’t kept God’s faithfulness and loyal love a private secret but shared it with everyone. Testimony is meant to be borne.

f.w: I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart

n: Since David hasn’t held back praise, he asks God not to hold back mercy. May God’s love and faithfulness guard him always.
Without warning, the psalm turns to distress: countless troubles and his own sins surround him, more than the hairs on his head. Even after deliverance, new trials come.

f.w: I am not able to look up

n: Verses 13–17 appear again, almost word for word, as Psalm 70. David pleads for God to hurry.
He asks that those trying to destroy him be driven back in confusion.
May the mockers who taunt him with “Aha, aha!” be stunned by their own shame.
In contrast, may all who seek God rejoice and keep saying, “The Lord is great!”
David admits he is poor and needy — yet the Lord is thinking about him. The closing plea: don’t delay.
